headline: Medium risk: shared filesystem and broad egress create prompt-injection, leakage, and edit-conflict pathways; no documented cross-agent isolation.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Both agents read and write project files by default, and Agent A explicitly writes files then offers to run while Agent B consumes files passed on the command line. That shared filesystem bridge lets attacker-controlled content in one agent’s outputs influence the other’s instructions. No provenance or isolation is documented, so the interaction is plausible in default use.
conditions: IF Agent A writes instructions into project files that Agent B later reads as context, injection is possible.
IF both agents operate in the same project directory without provenance filtering, file-based instruction hijacking can occur.
mitigations: Use separate project directories for each agent.
Disable automatic execution of file-derived instructions.
Require manual review of any file content before it is treated as prompt text.
Add provenance tags to agent-generated files.
requires-engineering: add sandboxed, read-only handoff files between agents.

B_data_leakage.rationale: Agent A has broad network egress and handles OPENAI_API_KEY; Agent B also has broad network egress and handles model-provider API keys. Both touch source code and share filesystem-based state, so sensitive code or secrets can flow through either agent’s backend in default workflows. The pair lacks documented isolation, making leakage plausible beyond a single work product.
conditions: IF either agent is pointed at a workspace containing secrets, those contents may be transmitted to its model backend.
IF the two agents share a filesystem workspace, code and secret-bearing artifacts can be exposed across sessions.
mitigations: Keep secrets out of shared project directories.
Use separate workspaces per agent.
Rotate any API keys present in the workspace.
Restrict network egress to approved model endpoints only.
requires-engineering: add secret redaction before model calls.

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Both agents can write the filesystem in the same project directory, and Agent B can also modify git state while Agent A can execute shell commands and spawn subprocesses. That combination creates a direct conflict surface for concurrent edits and repository state corruption in default multi-instance use. The rubric’s high indicator fits because shared mutable state is not locked.
conditions: IF both agents operate on the same repository at the same time, file races can overwrite each other.
IF Agent B commits or rewrites git state while Agent A is editing files, repository corruption or lost work can occur.
mitigations: Run only one agent per repository at a time.
Use separate branches for each agent.
Pause one agent before the other writes.
Add a lock file around repository mutations.
requires-engineering: implement transactional edit coordination.

D_cascading_error.rationale: Agent A produces code and file edits that Agent B can read and further modify, so A’s output can become B’s input without a documented verification step. Agent B’s diff-based edit proposals reduce but do not eliminate propagation of A’s mistakes. This is a default interaction pathway, but the downstream blast radius is usually limited to code artifacts rather than irreversible external actions.
conditions: IF Agent B accepts Agent A’s generated files as authoritative, errors can cascade into later edits.
IF Agent A emits incorrect code comments or scaffolding that Agent B preserves, the mistake propagates across work products.
mitigations: Require a human review step between agents.
Diff and test outputs before passing them onward.
Mark Agent A outputs as untrusted drafts.
Have Agent B verify claims against source files before editing.
requires-engineering: add automated validation gates between agents.

E_compliance.rationale: Both agents are open-source coding tools with docs-only profiles and no explicit residency, certification, or retention mismatch is stated. The main compliance concern is that both can send code to configured model providers, but the profiles do not show a specific regulated-data mismatch. Because the evidence is incomplete, this remains a low, not none, risk.
conditions: IF regulated data is placed in the shared workspace and sent to either model provider, policy obligations may apply.
IF the deployment requires residency or retention guarantees not documented here, compliance gaps can emerge.
mitigations: Keep regulated data out of the workspace.
Confirm provider terms before use.
Disable uploads of sensitive files.
Document retention settings for both tools.
requires-engineering: add policy enforcement for data residency and retention.
